headline: High: shared filesystem and overlapping write/network capabilities make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write the filesystem, use MCP, and ingest session files; gpt-researcher reads files and uses MCP/APIs. A shared workspace or MCP bridge could let attacker-controlled research content influence ECC instructions. This is not proven by direct interaction evidence, so uncertainty pushes to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or MCP server
IF gpt-researcher outputs are copied into ECC session files or prompts
mitigations: Separate workspaces and MCP endpoints for each agent
Disable MCP on one side for the test run
Add a manual review step before ECC consumes research output
Use read-only mounts for gpt-researcher inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-agent content

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, hooks, settings, git history, and security findings; gpt-researcher handles local documents, citations, and API-backed research. If they share a workspace, either agent can expose sensitive files to the other or to external APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared directory, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem or synced workspace
IF sensitive documents are placed in the research corpus
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Run gpt-researcher with a restricted input directory
Turn off external API calls for sensitive runs
Review ECC hooks and session retention settings before use
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, read files, spawn subprocesses, and install packages; ECC also modifies git state. In a shared repo or directory, concurrent writes can corrupt state or overwrite each other's outputs. Because the profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces by default, this is a high-risk conflict.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or output directory
IF either agent writes git-tracked files without locking
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Pause one agent while the other writes git state
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Keep package installation in isolated environments
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-researcher is explicitly planner/execution/publisher oriented, while ECC produces session summaries, skills, and security findings. That makes it plausible for one agent's output to become the other's input and then be acted on without strong verification. The pair therefore has a default pathway for error propagation and downstream amplification.
conditions: IF ECC consumes gpt-researcher reports as authoritative inputs
IF the publisher step acts on unreviewed research findings
mitigations: Require human review before publishing or committing outputs
Add a verification checklist for citations and claims
Limit ECC to summarization rather than action-taking
Separate planning and execution roles across runs
requires-engineering: add confidence gating between agents

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles session summaries, security findings, and retention-related secrets, while gpt-researcher processes local documents and external research APIs. If regulated or personal data enters the research flow, differing retention and API logging practices can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification conflict, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is included in research inputs
IF retention settings differ between ECC session files and gpt-researcher outputs
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Align retention settings before starting
Review API logging for both agents
Store outputs in a compliant location
requires-engineering: document a joint data-processing agreement
